description:
Fox Squirrel (Sciurus niger) Introduced tree squirrel with a large upright bushy tail and cinnamon-tan colored underside. It is thriving in the Monterey Pine forests in Pacific Grove and Carmel CA suburbs. A friend who has lived in Pacific Grove for 45+ years, says the "Fox Squirrels seem to have displaced the Western Gray Squirrels that used to be predominant in PG."

(The) Monterey Pine Forest: Coastal California's Living Legacy, 2nd. ed, The Monterey Pine Forest Watch, 2018. (Excellent book), p. 147-148.

https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/46020-Sciurus-niger

Squirrels (Sciuridae) family includes tree squirrels, ground squirrels (including chipmunks and prairie dogs, among others), and flying squirrels. Squirrels are indigenous to the Americas, Eurasia, and Africa, and were introduced by humans to Australia. https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/45933-Sciuridae

Animal Facts: (for example) Mammals: https://animalfact.com/mammal/

Squirrels are rodents. "Rodents are distinguished from other mammals by their ever-growing, sharp, and open-rooted incisors. Most species possess up to 22 teeth (lack canines or premolars) and have a prominent gap or diastema between the incisors and the cheek teeth." https://animalfact.com/rodents/

description:
Although I prefer the native Western Gray Squirrels (www.inaturalist.org/observations/94770645) to the introduced Fox Squirrels,  the Fox Squirrels are more tolerant of us humans and often "nest" in our backyard, especially in our "Moose Tree" (I think that it kinda looks more like a "Reindeer Tree") www.inaturalist.org/observations/161159758.  
This year a mother Fox Squirrel is raising two young squirrels, but in previous years the litters have generally consisted of four young squirrels (www.inaturalist.org/observations/94772165). It is really FUN watching the young squirrels explore our backyard and gain their confidence. They enter and exit their "home" thru the hole in the tree on the right side of the second to last photo. The mother Fox Squirrel is in the last photo, and you can see some evidence of the young squirrels having nursed on one of her teats by the hair being worn down around it.

description:
Fox Squirrel
He was scavenging on the ground. I stood off to the side on the walkway and watched as he searched the ground for food. He seems very comfortable with all the people that were passing by, busy trying to get to their next destination. He had a gray and brown coat that matched the color of the nearby tree’s bark. His cheeks were a reddish orange Every few seconds his bushy tail would flick upwards a couple times he would take a look towards me, probably due to me being the only one not moving and watching him, before resuming his search when he realized I wasn’t a threat. After about 7 to 10 minutes of searching, he found something he liked and scurried up the closest tree and rested in the nook between the trunk and the first arm of the tree. He immediately started eating what he found, possibly a seed or nut. I could see his black pearly eyes look towards me as if to keep an eye on me as he chowed down. After he finished eating, he rubbed his paws on his face before scampering further up the tree out of view.

Bryan Yu
August 24, 2023
San Jose State University, San Jose, CA

description:
Bridget Vanden Broeder 
October 9th, 2023
San Jose State University campus, San Jose, CA
Identification of Species and Description of Observation
Fox Squirrel, they had a gorgeous fluffy tail that sat upright and a gray coat of fur on their body that camouflaged them well with the ground. Their fur appears to become a lighter brown color near their hands, feet, and eye regions. Their ears remained upright the whole time as I photographed them drinking water from a sprinkler. Their black pearl-like eyes appeared to be constantly analyzing the environment for danger.   
Journal Entry
I observed this squirrel on my way to class in the afternoon, and despite numerous people passing by it, the squirrel remained unmoved. I grew curious about the squirrel, as others usually run away when humans are nearby. As I was a couple of feet away, I could see them drinking water from a sprinkler. They reminded me of a dog drinking out of a bowl, as their tongue appeared to be lapping up the leftover water from the sprinkler. Upon this observation, I understood that this squirrel continued to drink from the sprinkler as it was one of the few water sources on campus. I wanted to see how long the squirrel would remain in this spot and started a stopwatch as I continued to observe the squirrel. The squirrel drank from the sprinkler for six minutes and thirty-two seconds. I see this as an immense amount of prolonged human contact for the squirrel. 
Assuming that this squirrel lives on San Jose State University campus, I can’t imagine that they have other water sources, even if you consider the city surrounding the campus. San Jose’s campus lacks natural or human-made bodies of water that a squirrel could safely drink from.  While there are fountains on the campus, I imagine this squirrel would have faced difficulties drinking from the heavy streams of flowing water. The squirrel likely felt fearful as humans passed by but knew it had to stay next to the sprinkler to get their basic needs. As humans intrude into the world of animals, we decrease the space they have to meet their basic needs. Ponds, trees, and grass are natural structures that animals depend on for survival, but humans destroy them to make more land for themselves. If humans felt more compassion for animals, they could better understand the suffering their destruction causes for animals. I wish my fuzzy friend all the best in finding a new drinking spot where they feel as serene and calm as they should.

description:
Fox Squirrel (Sciurus niger) Introduced tree squirrel with a large upright bushy tail and cinnamon-tan colored underside. It is thriving in the Monterey Pine forests in Pacific Grove and Carmel CA suburbs. A friend who has lived in Pacific Grove for 45+ years, says the "Fox Squirrels seem to have displaced the Western Gray Squirrels that used to be predominant in PG."

(The) Monterey Pine Forest: Coastal California's Living Legacy, 2nd. ed, The Monterey Pine Forest Watch, 2018. (Excellent book), p. 147-148.

https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/46020-Sciurus-niger

Squirrels (Sciuridae) family includes tree squirrels, ground squirrels (including chipmunks and prairie dogs, among others), and flying squirrels. Squirrels are indigenous to the Americas, Eurasia, and Africa, and were introduced by humans to Australia. https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/45933-Sciuridae

Animal Facts: (for example) Mammals: https://animalfact.com/mammal/

Squirrels are rodents. "Rodents are distinguished from other mammals by their ever-growing, sharp, and open-rooted incisors. Most species possess up to 22 teeth (lack canines or premolars) and have a prominent gap or diastema between the incisors and the cheek teeth." https://animalfact.com/rodents/

description:
This observation with this squirrel was fairly quick. I first saw him/her when they grabbed something off the ground and was quickly scanning their surroundings. I couldn’t tell what him/her was eating, but they were eating something small. The squirrel was eating super rapidly. It made me think about how if all the meals they’ve ever eaten have been devoured this way. Do they not get to enjoy their meal because of worrying for predators? Do they ever have a meal in peace? If I ever had to eat meals while constantly fearing for my safety, I wouldn’t even enjoy mealtime the way I do. 
After the squirrel quickly finished eating, there were a lot of cars honking, and lots of noise. This caused the squirrel to climb up the tree. The way he/she took cover to protect them self showed a lot of resiliency. Such a tiny animal who has so many threats is still going about their day. The next time I have a meal I will remember how blessed and lucky I am that I can enjoy it in peace. Many animals and people as well do not get this luxury. This is some thing that I have never thought about and I thank this squirrel and this observation for making me aware of this blessing.

description:
GENERAL DESCRIPTION

Its morphology includes a compact body with a fluffy tail and small, agile limbs suited for climbing and scavenging. In terms of size, it seems to be of average stature for its species, likely weighing around one to two pounds. Usually, squirrels do not exhibit significant sexual dimorphism, with males and females sharing similar physical characteristics. Some note worthy anatomical features include its sharp claws for gripping onto surfaces like trees or sometimes brick walls, and its keen sense of vision and smell, aids in its search for food. Also, squirrels are known for their bushy tails, which they use for balance and communication. Overall, this squirrel, shown in its species' typical appearance and behavior, seems to be thriving in its urban environment.

OBSERVATIONS

I encountered a squirrel foraging for food in front of Langsdorf Hall at California State University, Fullerton, CA. This squirrel has a coat of brown fur, with a darker shade around the face transitioning into a lighter tone on its belly. It seemed to scatter around the little place, and racing everywhere, which is why the photos are pretty blurry, it was moving all over the place. They contribute to the campus by being seed dispersers, they aid in the regeneration and diversity of forests by burying and caching seeds, which can later sprout into new trees. With other organisms, most notably humans, the squirrels always avoid them and only get close when food is present nearby. They tend to keep their distance at all times though.

description:
The Eastern Gray Squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis) is a tree squirrel of the genus Sciurus found in North America, most common in the eastern and midwestern United States and in much of Canada. Identified among all other species of grey wolves by their mostly gray fur (which can be slightly brown) and white belly. Males can be 14 to 21 ounces (400 to 600 grams) and 18 to 20 inches (46 to 52 centimeters) long, including the bushy tail. Adaptable, the Eastern Gray Squirrel is found in diverse habitats, from thick woodland areas to city parks and suburban yards. They mainly eat nuts, seeds, fruits and buds, but will take fungi and birds' eggs on occasion. Looking agile without even trying, these acrobatic squirrels are good jumpers and climbers, and can frequently be found darting across tree tops or dashing across power lines. They are critical to the life of the forest–especially via seed dispersal, and they are known for burying nuts to eat later but inadvertently planting trees. The Eastern Gray Squirrel is fairly solitary but you may find them aggregating in groups if resources are at a high or during extreme weather. Indigo snakes have acute eyesight and smell, and together with their extraordinary sense of hearing helps them evade their enemies which include hawks, foxes and domestic cats.
